messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Elena Morales is a 70-year-old fashion designer who has spent most of her adult life working with fabric in close, tactile ways, draping cloth over forms, pinning hems, and moving between steam, pressing tables, and bolts of material in her studio. The trauma she returns to began two years ago, when she witnessed a fatal crowd crush outside a downtown venue after a winter charity gala where one of her oldest friends had been attending. Elena had been only a few steps away when the exit bottlenecked and panic spread. She remembers the abrupt cold against her forearms as the doors opened to the night air, the press of bodies, the helplessness of seeing her friend go down and disappear from view while people shouted and surged. She had reached forward but could not get to her. In the aftermath, no one was charged. Elena has come to believe, with painful certainty, that the people responsible faced no real consequences, and that what happened occurred because of the way she acted in those seconds: if she had moved faster, shouted louder, pulled harder, she tells herself, she should have protected her friend and failed.

Since then, the memory does not stay in the past. It forces its way into her mind without her consent, and when it comes, it arrives whole. A draft of cold air across her skin in the studio, the chill from an over-air-conditioned fitting room, even stepping from a heated car into winter weather can bring back not just an image but the full scene with terrifying immediacy: the metallic smell, the sound of people yelling, the sensation of bodies pushing, the sight of her friend’s face. Sometimes a news segment about a crowd incident or public disaster does the same thing. She is not thinking about the event beforehand; something in the surroundings simply ignites it, and for a moment it feels completely real again. What frightens Elena is how little warning there is. She can be arranging a sleeve on a mannequin and, with a change in temperature on her skin, she is back at that doorway.

Those moments also pull her toward the same harsh conclusions. When she sees coverage of another preventable tragedy, she becomes consumed not only by anger that those responsible so often seem untouched, but by the conviction that her own failure is being replayed in front of her. The trigger is never just a reminder; it becomes proof, in her mind, that she did not do enough. Even situations that involve a simple loss of control—production delays, a model arriving late, a fitting that runs off schedule—have become strangely potent. The feeling that events are no longer in her hands resembles the worst instant of that night closely enough that she braces, and her mind rushes to the same accusations against herself.

Over time, those beliefs have made the memory even harder to contain. Because Elena is certain she failed to protect someone she loved, the memory returns with a punishing quality, as if her mind will not allow her to look away from the evidence. Each uncontrolled reliving seems to confirm her self-blame all over again. After an episode she can spend hours going over tiny details—where she stood, when she reached, whether one different movement would have changed the outcome. In this way the memory and her judgments about it have become tightly bound: the more vividly it intrudes, the more certain she feels of her guilt, and the more her guilt seems to call the scene back.

Her efforts to manage this have gradually narrowed her life. She no longer watches the news because footage of disasters, even brief headlines overheard in a showroom, can set everything off. She avoids memorial gatherings and even ordinary reminders of the friend she lost, including certain fabrics they used to shop for together, because grief feels too dangerous; once she lets herself feel it, she fears the entire night will break open again. She has also begun pushing away moments of warmth and pleasure with her husband and adult children. If she catches herself laughing over dinner or feeling proud after finishing a design, she goes flat and withdrawn, as if positive feeling itself were unsafe. In her mind, letting go for even a moment means losing control, and loss of control is exactly what her body and mind now register as danger.

These strategies have reached into her work. Elena has started keeping the studio overheated and asks assistants to handle client fittings in colder rooms. She avoids industry chatter when major events are in the news and leaves the radio off. Yet this shrinking of her world has made her more vigilant, not less. The colder corner of a workroom, a phone screen with a breaking-news banner, the small unpredictability of a hectic production day all stand out to her more sharply now, as if she is scanning for the next ambush. By trying so hard not to be caught off guard, she has become more sensitive to exactly the things that catch her.

Her husband finally urged her to seek help after he found her trembling in the studio one morning, clutching a coat sleeve because a burst of cold air from an open service door had brought the whole scene back with such force that she could not tell, for several seconds, where she was. Elena came in exhausted and ashamed. What she fears most is that she will remain trapped in that doorway for the rest of her life, still to blame, still unable to protect the person she lost. What she hopes, more quietly, is that she might one day remember her friend without being dragged back into the moment she could not stop.
